Hebrews stands apart in the New Testament. It is a substantial, carefully argued work, written in some of the finest Greek in the New Testament. It begins without a greeting, like a sermon rather than a letter, and only at the very end does it turn into a letter, with personal news and greetings. The author calls it a word of exhortation, a sermon written down and sent to a congregation the author knew and hoped to visit again.

The letter does not name its writer. He says that the message of salvation was confirmed to him and his readers by those who heard the Lord, and he writes as one steeped in the Greek translation of the Old Testament, a teacher and pastor who knew ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧, and who cared deeply for his readers.

The title, to the Hebrews, was added early in the book's history, and it fits the contents. The readers were Jewish believers who knew the Scriptures of Israel well, along with the priesthood, the sacrifices and the tabernacle. The whole argument assumes that these things matter to them. The letter closes with greetings from those from ⟦l:italy_601|Italy⟧. It was written in the years before the temple in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ was destroyed in the year seventy, while the old sacrifices were still being offered.

What was happening to these believers? In their early days they had suffered for their faith. They had been publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution, they had stood by those in prison, and they had joyfully accepted the seizure of their property. That had not yet cost any of them their lives. But now, some time later, their enthusiasm was fading. Some had stopped meeting together. They were in danger of drifting, and of turning back from Christ to the familiar forms of worship they had known before, in which so much of their heritage was bound up. The writer's whole purpose is to keep them from falling away.

His method is to show, from their own Scriptures, that everything they valued has been surpassed and fulfilled in ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧. He is greater than the angels through whom the law was given, greater than ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, and greater than ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧, who led Israel into the land but did not give them lasting rest. Above all, he is the great high priest, appointed not in the line of ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ but in the order of ⟦p:melchisedec_1991|Melchizedek⟧, the mysterious priest king who blessed ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧ in Genesis. He serves in a better sanctuary, under a better covenant, the new covenant promised through ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧, and he has offered a better sacrifice, once for all, by offering himself.

The book moves back and forth between teaching and warning. Every so often the writer breaks off from his argument to plead with his readers, and some of these warnings are among the most solemn passages in the Bible. Then, after the long central section on priesthood and sacrifice, the tone changes. He calls up a great procession of men and women from Israel's history who lived by faith without seeing the promise fulfilled, from ⟦p:abel_13|Abel⟧ to the prophets, and urges his readers to run their own race with endurance. The book closes with practical instructions about life together, and a final blessing.

For a listener who has come through the Old Testament, Hebrews draws on almost all of it. It quotes the Psalms again and again, returns to the tabernacle of Exodus and the sacrifices of Leviticus, and revisits the wilderness generation and the patriarchs of Genesis. It is, in a sense, a guided reading of the Old Testament from the far side of the cross.
1:
Hebrews has no greeting. It opens with a single long sentence, carefully built, about the way God has spoken. In the past he spoke to the fathers through the prophets, at many times and in many ways. Now, in these last days, he has spoken by his Son. The writer then lays out who this Son is: heir of all things, the one through whom the universe was made, the radiance of God's glory, who made purification for sins and then sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.

That last phrase comes from Psalm one hundred and ten, which will return again and again throughout the book.

The rest of the chapter makes a comparison that may seem surprising at first: the Son is far greater than the angels. The law itself had been spoken through angels, as the next chapter recalls, and the writer builds his case from a chain of Old Testament quotations, mostly from the Psalms, which he reads as God himself speaking to and about his Son.
2:
The comparison with the angels is not finished, but first the writer pauses for the first of his warnings. If the message delivered through angels, the law, carried real consequences, how much more serious it would be to neglect the salvation announced by the Lord himself. The danger he names is drifting, like a boat slipping away from its moorings. The writer also mentions, in passing, that this message came to him and his readers through those who had heard the Lord.

Then he returns to his argument, and to a puzzle. Psalm eight speaks of human beings crowned with glory and given rule over everything. Yet that is not what we see in the world. What we do see, the writer says, is ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, made for a little while lower than the angels, and now crowned because he suffered death.

The rest of the chapter explains why the Son had to share fully in human flesh and blood: to break the power of death, and to become like his brothers in every way. The chapter ends by introducing, for the first time, the title that will dominate the book. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is a merciful and faithful high priest.
3:
Having shown that the Son is greater than the angels, the writer turns to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, the greatest figure in Israel's history, through whom God gave the law. He does not belittle Moses. Moses was faithful in all God's house, he says, as a servant. But ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is faithful over that house as a Son, and as its builder.

From ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ the writer moves naturally to the generation Moses led out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧. He quotes at length from Psalm ninety-five, a psalm still sung in synagogue and church, which recalls the rebellion of the Israelites in the wilderness. That generation saw God's works for forty years, yet hardened their hearts, and God swore that they would not enter his rest. Their bodies fell in the desert, as the book of Numbers records.

The writer presses the point home. The word today in the psalm, he says, still speaks. His readers, like the Israelites, have been brought out and are on their way, and the danger is the same: an unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God. He urges them to encourage one another daily, as long as it is still called today.
4:
The writer is still reflecting on Psalm ninety-five and its warning that the wilderness generation would never enter God's rest. Now he asks what that rest really is. It cannot simply be the land of Canaan, he argues, because long after ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ led the people into the land, God was still speaking through the psalm about entering his rest today. So the promise remains open.

He links this rest with the seventh day of creation, when God rested from all his works, and concludes that a Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God. The readers are urged to make every effort to enter it.

The chapter then turns on two memorable passages. The first describes the word of God as living and active, sharper than any double-edged sword, laying bare the thoughts of the heart. The second returns to the high priest introduced at the end of chapter two. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has passed through the heavens, and he is able to sympathise with weakness, because he was tempted in every way and yet was without sin.
5:
The writer now begins the long central theme of the book: ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ as high priest. He starts with what every Jewish reader would know about the office. A high priest is chosen from among the people, to act for them before God and offer sacrifices for sins, including his own. And no one takes the honour for himself. He must be called by God, as ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ was.

So it was with Christ, the writer says, and he brings together two psalms. The first, Psalm two, calls him God's Son. The second, Psalm one hundred and ten, calls him a priest forever, in the order of ⟦p:melchisedec_1991|Melchizedek⟧. That name will be the key to the next few chapters. The writer adds a moving glimpse of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧'s earthly life, praying with loud cries and tears to the one who could save him from death.

Then he stops. He has much more to say about this, he tells his readers, but it is hard to explain, because they have become dull of hearing. By now they should be teachers, yet they need milk again, like infants, rather than solid food.
6:
The writer has just rebuked his readers for needing milk rather than solid food. He now urges them to leave the elementary teachings behind and move on towards maturity.

What follows is one of the most solemn warnings in the New Testament. The writer warns that it is impossible to restore to repentance those who have been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, and then fallen away. Then, after a picture of land that drinks in the rain and bears either a crop or thorns, the writer softens his tone. He is convinced of better things in his readers' case. God has not forgotten their love and their service to the saints, and he wants them to show the same diligence to the end.

To steady them, he goes back to ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧. When God made his promise to Abraham, he confirmed it with an oath, swearing by himself. That hope, the writer says, is an anchor for the soul, reaching behind the curtain into the ⟦l:most_holy_place_827|inner sanctuary⟧, where ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has gone ahead as a high priest in the order of ⟦p:melchisedec_1991|Melchizedek⟧. With that phrase he is ready, at last, to explain what he means.
7:
The writer now explains the figure he has been pointing to for two chapters. ⟦p:melchisedec_1991|Melchizedek⟧ appears only briefly in the Old Testament. In Genesis fourteen, after ⟦p:abraham_58|Abram⟧, as he was still called, rescues his nephew ⟦p:lot_1830|Lot⟧ from a coalition of kings, a king of ⟦l:salem_1018|Salem⟧ who is also a priest of God Most High comes out to meet him, blesses him, and receives a tenth of everything. Centuries later, Psalm one hundred and ten speaks of a king who is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.

The writer draws out the significance of both passages. He notes the meaning of the name, king of righteousness, and of ⟦l:salem_1018|Salem⟧, peace, and observes that Genesis records no parents, genealogy, birth or death for ⟦p:melchisedec_1991|Melchizedek⟧. And he argues that because ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧ gave him a tenth and received his blessing, Melchizedek is greater than Abraham, and greater, therefore, than ⟦p:levi_1820|Levi⟧ and the priests descended from him.

This matters because ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ came from the tribe of Judah, not from the priestly tribe of ⟦p:levi_1820|Levi⟧. His priesthood rests not on descent but on the power of an indestructible life, and on God's oath. Unlike the priests who died and were replaced, he lives forever, and he offered his sacrifice once for all.
8:
The writer pauses to sum up. The point of everything he has been saying, he tells his readers, is that we do have such a high priest, seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven.

Now he widens the comparison from the priest to the place where he serves, and the covenant under which he serves. The priests on earth minister in a sanctuary that is only a copy and shadow of the heavenly one. He recalls the instruction given to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ on ⟦l:mount_sinai_855|Mount Sinai⟧, to make the tabernacle according to the pattern he was shown on the mountain.

The heart of the chapter is the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament. It comes from the prophet ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧, who spoke in the last years before ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ fell to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, and who promised that the days were coming when God would make a new covenant with Israel and Judah. Under it God would write his laws on their hearts and remember their sins no more. The writer draws a simple conclusion: by calling this covenant new, God has made the first one old.
9:
Having introduced the new covenant, the writer turns to the worship of the old one, and he takes his readers back to the tabernacle described in the book of Exodus. He walks through it briefly: the outer room, the Holy Place, with its lampstand, table and consecrated bread, and then, behind the second curtain, the Most Holy Place, with the ark of the covenant and the cherubim above the mercy seat.

He focuses on one moment in Israel's year, the Day of Atonement described in Leviticus. Only once a year did the high priest go into the inner room, and never without blood. For the writer, that closed curtain says that the way into God's presence had not yet been opened.

Against that background he sets the work of Christ. Christ has entered not a man-made sanctuary but heaven itself, and not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, once for all. The writer recalls how ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ sealed the first covenant with blood at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, and he looks ahead to the day when Christ will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who wait for him.
10:
The writer brings his long argument about sacrifice to its conclusion. The law, he says, is only a shadow of the good things to come. Sacrifices offered year after year could never take away sins, or they would have stopped. He quotes Psalm forty, in which the speaker tells God that sacrifices are not what he desired, and says, here I am, I have come to do your will. The writer hears these words on the lips of Christ, whose one offering has made perfect for all time those being sanctified.

With that, the argument turns to appeal. Since the way into the Most ⟦l:holy_place_575|Holy Place⟧ is now open, the readers are to draw near to God, hold fast their hope, and not give up meeting together, as some have started to do.

Then comes another sombre warning about those who deliberately keep on sinning after receiving the truth. But the writer follows it, as before, with encouragement. He reminds his readers of their early days, when they endured public insult, cared for prisoners, and joyfully accepted the seizure of their property. He urges them not to throw away their confidence now, and ends with words from the prophet ⟦p:habakkuk_1334|Habakkuk⟧: my righteous one will live by faith.
11:
The last chapter ended with the word faith, and this chapter takes it up. It opens with a short description of what faith is, the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen. Then it unrolls one of the best known passages in the Bible, a procession of men and women from Israel's history, each introduced with the same words: by faith.

Almost every name will be familiar. The roll begins with ⟦p:abel_13|Abel⟧, ⟦p:enoch_1192|Enoch⟧ and ⟦p:noah_2210|Noah⟧ from the early chapters of Genesis, and lingers longest over ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧ and ⟦p:sarah_2473|Sarah⟧, who lived as strangers in the promised land, looking for a better country. It moves on through ⟦p:isaac_616|Isaac⟧, ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧ and ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧, then to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and the exodus, the fall of ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧, and ⟦p:rahab_2388|Rahab⟧.

Then the pace quickens. The writer says he has no time to tell of ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧, ⟦p:barak_401|Barak⟧, ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧, ⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧, ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ and the prophets, and he gathers the rest into a rush of brief allusions to victories, rescues, sufferings and martyrdoms. The chapter's final note is that none of them received what was promised. God had planned something better, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us.
12:
The great procession of chapter eleven now becomes a great cloud of witnesses surrounding them, and the readers are runners on the track. The writer urges them to throw off every weight and run with endurance, their eyes fixed on ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, who endured the cross and has sat down at the right hand of God.

He speaks frankly about their present hardships. Quoting the book of Proverbs, he tells them to understand their suffering as the discipline a father gives the son he loves. They have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood, he notes, a hint that none of them has yet died for the faith.

Then comes a warning drawn from Genesis, the story of ⟦p:esau_1216|Esau⟧, who sold his birthright for a single meal and could not afterwards win back the blessing. The chapter ends with two contrasting mountains. Israel came to ⟦l:mount_sinai_855|Mount Sinai⟧, with its fire, darkness and trembling. The readers have come to ⟦l:mount_zion_860|Mount Zion⟧, the heavenly ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, with its angels, its assembly and its mediator of a new covenant. The writer closes with a quotation from the prophet ⟦p:haggai_1349|Haggai⟧ about God shaking heaven and earth once more, and with a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
13:
The great argument of Hebrews is complete, and the final chapter turns to the practical life of the community. The instructions come quickly: brotherly love, hospitality to strangers, care for those in prison, faithfulness in marriage, contentment rather than love of money. The writer asks them to remember their former leaders, who first taught them, and to imitate their faith.

One last time he returns to the language of sacrifice and the tabernacle. He warns against strange teachings about foods, and notes that the bodies of the animals sacrificed on the Day of Atonement were burned outside the camp. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ too suffered outside the city gate, and the readers are to go out to him and share his disgrace.

The closing lines are those of a letter. The writer asks for prayer and hopes to be restored to his readers soon. He offers a final blessing, calling ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ the great Shepherd of the sheep. And he adds a few lines of news: ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ has been released, and the writer hopes to come with him. Those from ⟦l:italy_601|Italy⟧ send their greetings.
